94.history: The small citadel port far off on the south-east coast keeps its mills on its river. In a wet spring in LE 244 the river broke its banks and carried away the lower mills, and the mill-wrights built them again on the higher ground; a pupil of Òrd an t-Seabhaig house at Ros gheal who saw it called the flood a kind of overfed hawk, and Gormshuil nic Artair told him a river was a river, and sent him back to watch the mills rebuilt before he judged further. At the end of the age's first year the question whether anyone would go with the fleet was asked at hearths from Baile chrom in the north-west as far as Seann Vell.
94.known_for: its mills, and the flood of LE 244

422.history: Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land about the city in the eastern hills, walled it in stone in LE 261 without the crown's leave, the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house. Queen Sìleas summoned their head to a cold supper at An Talla Dearg; neither spoke of the walls, both understood, and the walls stood. The smiths of the city made the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses from the layered steel of their fellowship, folded and refolded, until in LE 1,568 the fellowship lost the last smith who knew the folding well enough to finish a blade alone; the blades made after him were ordinary work.
422.known_for: the walls of Clann Ìomhair, and the layered steel lost

315.history: The old hall at Dùn ìseal, where Brìde's flame burns in Talla na Lasrach and the stone cup stands on the threshold, was the heir of the custody before Taigh na Fèithe took it; in this age it is the seat of Na Seann Spioradan of the eastern shires. In LE 179 their keepers raised a house for the ancestors there and cut the names of the eastern dead on wooden posts, renewed each generation; a young man of Clann Fhearchair, reading them, said a shire that trusted wood to hold its dead must trust its memory further than he would. Lightning burned the posts to their footings in LE 1,149, and the keepers cut the names again from memory and from Leabhar a' Chùraim, owning in their roll that some were guesses. An earthquake cracked the spirit-house in LE 1,649 and killed no one; the keepers took it for a warning and could not agree of what.

398.history: The quarry village of the south-east burned in LE 446 when fire ran through its thatch, and most of it went. King Aonghas sent what the crown's granaries could spare before the winter closed the roads. A quarryman's household was the first to roof again in slate, judging that a man who cut the stone had less excuse than his neighbours to sleep under straw, and the village was rebuilt in slate from the quarries nearby and known for its slate roofs from then on.

326.history: The southern mill town became the southernmost house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in the sixth century of the count. Its bell-founders cast the first bronze bell on Dia-thìr to hang in a hawk-house in LE 514, with King Tormod Bàn standing at the casting; it cracked in its first frost, and the second, thicker at the waist, held, and rang at every measured burning. There Òrd an t-Seabhaig's teaching was still given whole and unsoftened when it faded elsewhere, and pilgrims came to it from further south than any hawk-house had drawn from before.
326.known_for: the first bell of a hawk-house

256.history: The citadel town in the eastern hills sends its drovers over the hills each year with cattle for the mining towns; from LE 484 they marked their road with a cairn at every day's stage, the first roads on the island so marked, so that a beast lost in mist or a driver new to the trade might find the way again. A boundary dispute at Àth chiar was still unsettled after three seasons when Tormod Bàn lay dying, and his last clear order gave it to the custodians to finish. In the sixteenth century its drovers took their beasts to the fair at Baile Mòr ruadh instead of selling nearer home.

233.history: The hill-lords of Baile ghorm walled a pale hill above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada in the third century of the count, and in LE 1,051 set a single market there to gather the south-east's scattered trade into one place. Its rare good was the pearls of the south-eastern shallows, sold in whole parcels as at no other market; at the first opening the shore-woman Sìne nic Ruairidh brought a whole season's gathering rather than sell it a pearl at a time along the road, and a trader of Cathair mhòr paid her more for the lot than she had ever been offered piecemeal.
233.known_for: the market above the mill-race, and its pearls

3.history: The south-eastern town's dyers made a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own, and in LE 1,064 the dyer Oighrig nic Ailein, after ten years changing one thing at a time, found the mixing that held the blue through washing after washing; cloth of it was worn at Taigh na Fèithe's midwinter gathering within the year and became the feast-day dress of the custodian houses. The last dyer who knew the mordant quarrelled with both her apprentices and died without teaching either, and the blue that followed, though it kept the old name, was the common blue of the rest of the island; the old weavers held the two lengths side by side and mourned the difference aloud for the rest of their lives.
3.known_for: the Baile ghorm blue, and its losing

466.history: The south-eastern mill town took the swallowing cough in LE 1,079, a sickness that closed the throat until a man could not swallow his own spit; it went house by house along the lower street and up into the hill lanes, and the town lost near a third of its people. Beathag Fhionn, crowned in LE 1,082, shut the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain within the month and set a reeve at each of its six fords, and the road stayed shut three years; the cough never crossed west of them. The town stood at less than two households in three for twenty years and more, its old reeve walking the lower street once a season to write down which roofs had fallen, until families from the hill country above came down a handful a year and took the empty houses by lot.
466.known_for: the swallowing cough, and the houses taken by lot

110.history: The walled port of the south-east was the second town the swallowing cough reached, in LE 1,081. Its townsfolk closed the harbour themselves before any order came, and kept the shared meal by leaving food at the town gate for the households that could no longer come to the board. The coast road from it to Muileann dhomhain was shut by the queen's reeves for three years after.
110.known_for: the harbour shut against the cough, and the meal at the gate

288.history: White-stone millers raised the mill town in the south-east in LE 1,082 to grind for the city of Dùn dhearg. Its potters of Clann Mhic Phàil made a grey-green glaze that no other kiln could match, and the custodian houses bought their table-ware from that one family; the secret went mother to daughter unwritten. The last of the family, Iain Mac Phàil, took two apprentices in his last years, and neither learned to judge the moment the kiln's heat must be let fall. He died without passing it on in LE 1,509, and for a generation the town's potters tried to match it and failed.
288.known_for: the grey-green glaze, and its losing
